newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia sees increased access for sugar exports.
newsitem.headline: Australia sees increased access for sugar exports.

text.p: Australia hoped to see a substantial increase in its sugar exports to Egypt next year and hoped to supply at least 250,000 tonnes to Saudi Arabia, Deputy Prime Minister and Trade Minister Tim Fischer said on Wednesday.

The Australian government also had a range of market access issues before it in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) group, particularly in the Philippines and Indonesia, he told the 1997 Australian Sugar Convention.
"Among the most contentious issues are the possible increase in the sugar tariff in the Philippines (and) the impact of state trading arrangements for Indonesia's imports," he said.

Also included were the high level of protection in competitors such as Thailand and the European Union and the threat of a possible decrease in Australia's share of the U.S. sugar quota as a result of access being sought by Mexico under NAFTA (the North American Free Trade Area) provisions, he said.
"We are very much alive to these threats and, with industry, working to protect our interests," he said.
Improvement was in prospect on the substantial tariff and other barriers faced by the Australian sugar export industry, he said.

Countries now within the range of zero to five percent included Brunei, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Israel, Kazakhstan, Kuwait, Latvia, Malaysia, New Zealand, Singapore, Slovenia and the United Arab Emirates, all at zero, he said.
Bulgaria, Egypt and South Korea were on five percent tariffs, Canada offered Australia duty free preference while Jordan had recently dropped its tariff to five percent from 50 percent, he said.
The zero to five percent tariff range countries covered 60 percent of Australia's sugar exports, he said.
In other key markets, Japan had just lowered its tariff to 15 yen per kg, while in China better access for sugar was a high priority in World Trade Organisation (WTO) negotiations, Fischer said.
In the U.S., the Australian government continued to push for fundamental reform of the sugar regime. Australia had benefited from a quota increase this year.

In Taiwan, where Australia was the dominant supplier, last year's interim access package secured for Australia guaranteed levels of access from the time of Taiwan's accession to the WTO together with halving of the tariff to 12.5 percent, he said.
In Bulgaria's WTO accession negotiations last year Australia secured a tariff quota commitment of 250,000 tonnes at a maximum tariff of five percent, Fischer said.

In future multilateral negotiations Australia would seek to negotiate on the basis of its Uruguay Round tariff ceiling of seven cents per kg. This would provide significant negotiating coin for future negotiations, he said.
Australia also would be seeking credit for tariff removals in its Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum negotiations, he said.
